# OCP 2026: Agentic AI Drives the Data Center's Chip-to-Grid Transformation

## Key Highlights

- OCP is extending its standards mission from servers and racks to the full AI infrastructure stack, encompassing silicon, cooling, power distribution, facilities and utility-grid integration.

- AMD introduced its Helion agentic AI rack, while Arm and NVIDIA outlined new CPU architectures and infrastructure requirements for rapidly expanding autonomous workloads.

- Meta detailed the engineering behind its Prometheus AI cluster in Ohio, including fabric structures, new optical networking, open-source transport software and AI-optimized concrete.

- Broadcom and NVIDIA presented advances in Ethernet networking and optical interconnects designed to overcome the growing physical constraints of accelerator clusters.

- New OCP data center and grid-resilience specifications, along with NVIDIA's advances in dynamic power management, signal a shift toward treating the AI factory as a coordinated, grid-aware infrastructure system.

The fabric-roofed keynote hall at OCP 2026 in San Jose was built by Sprung Structures, the same company supplying massive engineered enclosures for Meta’s Prometheus AI campus in Ohio. Meta’s Santosh Janardhan noted that the approach can help bring data center capacity online in just three to five months, versus years for conventional construction.

Standing before thousands of engineers and technology executives at the opening of the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit in San Jose, Meta's Santosh Janardhan pointed to the enormous fabric structure surrounding the audience.

It was, he explained, an example of the same construction technology Meta had begun deploying to accelerate its massive AI infrastructure buildout.

At the company's Prometheus AI cluster in New Albany, Ohio, traditional assumptions about data center construction had given way to an urgent question: What if the next generation of AI infrastructure could be built in months rather than years, using engineered fabric structures instead of conventional concrete-and-steel buildings?

"We are actually also training a model while we were building it," said Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure.

The presentation offered a striking illustration of the larger message emerging from Monday's opening keynotes: The AI factory is becoming a fundamentally different kind of data center.

Across presentations by AMD, Meta, Arm, Broadcom and NVIDIA, a common theme emerged. The rapid expansion of AI inference and autonomous agents is forcing new approaches to computing, networking, construction, power distribution and operations. At the same time, the diversity of silicon architectures and the enormous physical scale of deployments are making common infrastructure specifications increasingly important.

The result is a significant expansion of OCP's original mission.

Fifteen years after the organization began applying open-source principles to hardware design, the industry's next challenge is developing interoperable infrastructure across the entire data center, from processor architecture to the utility connection.

## OCP's New Mandate: From Chip to Grid

OCP CEO George Tchaparian opened the summit by describing an organization whose scale increasingly reflects the industry's transformation.

This year's event attracted approximately 15,000 attendees, with another 3,000 on a waitlist. Tchaparian said OCP expects membership to exceed 700 organizations by year-end, while technical contributions are growing approximately 30% annually.

The organization has already announced that its 2027 Global Summit will move to San Francisco's Moscone Center to accommodate further growth.

More consequential than the attendance figures, however, is the widening scope of OCP's work.

Originally centered on open server designs, racks and supporting hardware, the organization's roadmap now encompasses facilities infrastructure, liquid cooling, power distribution, firmware, security, networking and the increasingly complex connections between data centers and utilities.

Tchaparian characterized the emerging approach as "chip-to-grid" infrastructure.

This reflects a fundamental engineering problem. As hyperscalers and AI infrastructure providers deploy increasingly specialized processors, the electrical, thermal and mechanical consequences of those design decisions extend well beyond individual servers.

Higher accelerator densities require new cooling strategies. New power architectures affect rack configurations and electrical distribution. Faster networks alter equipment layouts and cable requirements. Different silicon designs can introduce entirely new facility-level constraints.

The traditional process of designing computing equipment and adapting data centers to accommodate it is increasingly difficult to sustain at AI scale.

OCP is therefore emphasizing what Tchaparian called co-optimized data centers: infrastructure in which silicon, racks, networking, cooling and power systems are developed with common interfaces and shared design objectives.

The challenge is compounded by growing silicon diversity. Hyperscalers are developing custom accelerators alongside commercial GPUs and CPUs, increasing the risk of fragmented hardware ecosystems that require repeated engineering across otherwise similar facilities.

OCP also intends to extend hyperscale-derived standards into what it calls the AI computing continuum, encompassing neocloud providers, colocation operators, enterprises and geographically distributed inference infrastructure.

The objective is not to eliminate architectural differentiation. It is to reduce the amount of infrastructure that must be redesigned every time the underlying computing technology changes.

## Agentic AI Gives the CPU a New Mission

One of the most consequential themes of the opening keynotes was the renewed importance of general-purpose computing.

AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su described 2026 as the year of inference, estimating that inference now represents approximately 60% of the AI computing market.

She pointed to an approximately 14-fold increase in agentic AI traffic during the year, reflecting the accelerating adoption of systems that do more than respond to individual prompts.

Instead, autonomous agents can plan tasks, invoke software tools, execute code, retrieve information and coordinate multiple model interactions.

These operations create substantial demand for CPUs, even as GPUs remain essential to model training and inference.

For infrastructure designers, this introduces a distinction between generating AI tokens and executing the work those tokens initiate.

An agent may use a GPU-accelerated language model to determine its next action, but that action can require dedicated CPU resources, memory, networking, storage and secure execution environments.

Multiply those activities across millions of persistent agents, and the computing requirements begin to look very different from those of traditional chatbot services.

Su said AMD has revised its estimated total addressable market for data center CPUs three times in nine months. The company now forecasts a market exceeding $200 billion by 2030, with annual growth approaching 50%.

Those are aggressive company projections, but they underscore the degree to which agentic computing is altering expectations for data center hardware demand.

"AI at scale is a team sport," Su said, emphasizing the importance of interoperability across CPUs, GPUs, purpose-built accelerators, networking and software.

### AMD Introduces Helion for Agentic Infrastructure

AMD used the summit to announce Helion , an open rack-scale reference design intended specifically for agentic AI workloads.

Unlike the company's Helios AI rack, which emphasizes tightly integrated GPU acceleration, Helion is designed to accommodate different combinations of CPU and GPU resources according to the applications being deployed.

Hyperscale configurations can use CPU-only racks alongside separate GPU inference systems. Enterprise configurations can combine CPUs and AMD Instinct GPUs within a single rack.

The architecture supports up to 32,768 sixth-generation EPYC CPU cores in its highest-density CPU-only configuration, while mixed configurations can incorporate AMD Instinct MI350P GPUs.

It also integrates a token router intended to direct model requests toward appropriate computing resources, reflecting the growing importance of matching individual AI tasks with suitable models and hardware.

Based on OCP rack specifications, Helion supports both air-cooled and liquid-cooled configurations. AMD plans to contribute the design to OCP, with partner-developed systems expected to become available beginning in November.

Su also provided an update on Helios , the company's existing rack-scale AI architecture developed in collaboration with Meta.

Helios incorporates 72 GPUs in a liquid-cooled rack weighing nearly 7,000 pounds. Production shipments began in September, according to Su, with initial installations at major AI customers and a broader manufacturing ramp planned through the first half of 2027.

The company also displayed its EPYC Verano processor, a 192-core design intended to improve power efficiency and CPU-to-GPU connectivity. Production is planned for the first half of 2027.

Together, these developments illustrate AMD's strategy of treating CPUs, GPUs and specialized accelerators as complementary components within increasingly configurable AI infrastructure.

### Arm: When AI Agents Become Virtual Users

Arm Executive Vice President Mohamed Awad approached the same transition from a different direction.

Awad argued that agentic AI fundamentally changes the relationship between computing infrastructure and its users.

Traditional cloud applications generally respond to requests initiated by people. Autonomous agents introduce virtual users capable of initiating tasks continuously, at machine speed.

That shift places new demands on the cloud-native systems supporting them.

Awad distinguished three increasingly important CPU functions: processors optimized to support AI accelerators, general-purpose cloud CPUs that operate infrastructure and services, and CPUs dedicated to executing agentic workloads.

The distinction also has implications for security.

Agents may execute software, access applications and handle sensitive information within persistent computing environments. Isolating those activities becomes essential as autonomous systems proliferate.

Arm announced a new white paper, developed with input from Fujitsu, Meta and OpenAI, examining how CPU performance should be evaluated for agentic applications.

Rather than relying exclusively on conventional processor benchmarks, the initiative seeks to establish performance measurements that better reflect the real-world behavior of AI agents.

Awad's central argument was that CPU performance can no longer be evaluated independently of the distributed services, memory resources and accelerated computing systems with which processors interact.

### NVIDIA Adds a Dedicated Vera CPU Rack

NVIDIA reinforced the same trend with a new Vera CPU rack architecture based on its MGX infrastructure specification.

The liquid-cooled design accommodates 256 Vera CPUs and targets agent execution, orchestration, tool calling and related computing workloads.

NVIDIA Vice President Ian Buck described the Vera CPU as an important component of the company's broader agentic computing architecture, citing significant per-core performance improvements over its previous Grace generation.

The company also outlined plans for Meta to deploy Vera-based CPU infrastructure.

Collectively, the AMD, Arm and NVIDIA presentations suggest an important shift in how AI data centers may be organized.
